title: Momentum, impulse and collisions
blurb: Calculate momentum and impulse, explain how air bags lower the force of a crash, and use conservation of momentum for collisions and recoil.
question: A 2,000 kg truck at 10 m/s strikes a parked 1,000 kg car and they lock together. How fast do they move off, was kinetic energy conserved, and why would an air bag protect the car's driver?

teach.body: Formally, momentum is the product of an object's mass and velocity: p = mv, measured in kg·m/s. It is a vector, pointing the same way as the velocity. In plain English: momentum is 'mass in motion', a measure of how hard something is to stop. A slow truck and a fast baseball can both be hard to stop: one has huge mass, the other high speed. Anything at rest has zero momentum.

Impulse is force multiplied by the time it acts: J = Ft, in N·s (the same as kg·m/s). Impulse equals the change in momentum: Ft = Δp. So a fixed change in momentum can come from a large force over a short time or a small force over a long time. Safety devices work by stretching the stopping time, which lowers the force. They do NOT reduce the change in momentum.

teach.caption: F = Δp ÷ t. Ten times the time gives one tenth of the force.

teach.body: In an isolated system (no outside net force), total momentum before an event equals total momentum after it. This holds for every collision and every explosion. Pick one direction as positive and give opposite motion a minus sign. Recoil is the explosion case: a system at rest has zero total momentum, so after a push the pieces move in opposite directions with equal-sized momenta (a rifle and bullet, a rocket and its exhaust).

teach.caption: Lost kinetic energy becomes heat, sound and deformation. Momentum is conserved in all three.

items: Stick together: a 2,000 kg truck at 10 m/s hits a parked 1,000 kg car. v = (2,000 × 10) ÷ 3,000 = 6.7 m/s.
Recoil: a 4.0 kg rifle fires a 0.010 kg bullet at 400 m/s. Bullet p = 4.0 kg·m/s, so the rifle moves back at 4.0 ÷ 4.0 = 1.0 m/s.
Opposite directions: 1.0 kg at +3.0 m/s meets 2.0 kg at −1.0 m/s and they stick. Total p = 3.0 − 2.0 = 1.0 kg·m/s; v = 1.0 ÷ 3.0 = +0.33 m/s.

teach.body: Tasha, a respiratory therapy applicant, catches a 0.20 kg softball moving at 30 m/s. Its momentum is 0.20 × 30 = 6.0 kg·m/s, and she must remove all of it. Stopping it in 0.050 s with a rigid glove takes 6.0 ÷ 0.050 = 120 N. Letting the glove ride back so the catch lasts 0.15 s cuts the force to 6.0 ÷ 0.15 = 40 N. Same impulse, one third of the force.

teach.text: Air bags do not reduce the change in momentum; they lengthen the time and so reduce the force. Momentum is conserved in inelastic collisions too; it is kinetic energy that is lost. Objects moving toward each other: subtract their momenta. And p = mv is not KE = ½mv²: doubling speed doubles p but quadruples KE.

items: Momentum p = mv (kg·m/s), a vector in the direction of motion.
Impulse J = Ft = Δp; a longer stopping time means a smaller force.
Isolated system: total momentum before = total momentum after.
Elastic: momentum and KE conserved. Inelastic: momentum only. Perfectly inelastic: objects stick.
Recoil from rest: equal and opposite momenta.

summary: You can now calculate momentum and impulse and explain how air bags, padding and soft hands lower the force by lengthening the stopping time. You can also apply conservation of momentum to sticking collisions, opposite-direction collisions and recoil, and tell elastic from inelastic collisions.

A.q: What is the SI unit of momentum?
A.why: p = mv, so the unit is kilograms × meters per second: kg·m/s (equal to N·s).

whyNot.0: kg·m/s² is the newton, the unit of force.
whyNot.2: Impulse is force × time (N·s), not force ÷ time.
whyNot.3: kg·m²/s² is the joule, the unit of energy.

A.q: What is the momentum of a 1,000 kg car moving at 20 m/s?

whyNot.0: Divides mass by speed instead of multiplying.
whyNot.1: Computes kinetic energy (½ × 1,000 × 20² = 200,000 J), not momentum.
whyNot.2: Halves the product; momentum has no ½ factor.

A.q: In which type of collision is kinetic energy conserved?
A.why: An elastic collision conserves both momentum and kinetic energy; the objects bounce apart with no energy lost to heat or deformation.

whyNot.0: Inelastic collisions conserve momentum but lose some kinetic energy.
whyNot.1: Objects that stick together lose the most kinetic energy.
whyNot.3: In an explosion stored energy becomes extra kinetic energy, so KE is not conserved.

B.q: A 60 kg skater and a 40 kg skater stand at rest on ice. They push apart, and the 40 kg skater moves off at 3.0 m/s. What is the 60 kg skater's velocity?
B.why: Total momentum stays zero. 40 × 3.0 = 120 kg·m/s, so the 60 kg skater has 120 kg·m/s the other way: v = 120 ÷ 60 = 2.0 m/s, opposite.

whyNot.1: Equal momenta, not equal speeds: the heavier skater moves more slowly.
whyNot.2: Starting from rest, the two must move in opposite directions to keep total momentum zero.

B.q: A 0.40 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m/s and is stopped, without bouncing, in 0.020 s. What average force does the wall exert on it?

whyNot.0: Multiplies the momentum change by the time instead of dividing.
whyNot.1: Divides speed by time (10 ÷ 0.020) and leaves out the mass.
whyNot.3: 4.0 kg·m/s is the change in momentum, not the force.

B.q: Why do gymnasts land on thick, soft mats?
options: The mats cut the gymnast's change in momentum
The mats shorten landing time, reducing the force
The mats raise the impulse the gymnast receives
The mats lengthen landing time, reducing the force
B.why: The gymnast's change in momentum is fixed. Ft = Δp, so stretching the landing time lowers the average force.

whyNot.0: The gymnast still goes from moving to stopped; the mat changes the time, not Δp.
whyNot.1: A shorter time would raise the force, not lower it.
whyNot.2: Impulse equals the fixed change in momentum; the mat does not raise it.

C.q: A 1,500 kg car moving east at 20 m/s collides with a 2,500 kg van moving west at 10 m/s, and they lock together. What is their velocity just after the collision?

whyNot.0: Adds the momenta (55,000 ÷ 4,000) as if both moved east.
whyNot.2: Right size, wrong direction: the car had more momentum, so the wreck moves east.
whyNot.3: Divides by the car's mass alone (5,000 ÷ 1,500); the joined mass is 4,000 kg.

C.q: A 50 kg astronaut floating at rest throws a 2.0 kg tool away at 5.0 m/s. What is her recoil speed?
C.why: Tool p = 2.0 × 5.0 = 10 kg·m/s. She gets 10 kg·m/s the other way: v = 10 ÷ 50 = 0.20 m/s.

whyNot.0: Equal momenta, not equal speeds: she has 25 times the tool's mass.
whyNot.1: Divides the tool's speed by her mass (5.0 ÷ 50) and leaves out the tool's mass.

C.q: A 2.0 kg cart at 3.0 m/s hits an identical 2.0 kg cart at rest. After the collision the first cart is stopped. What is the second cart's speed?
C.why: Momentum before = 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0 kg·m/s, all of which passes to the second cart: v = 6.0 ÷ 2.0 = 3.0 m/s.

whyNot.1: 1.5 m/s would be the speed if the carts stuck together; here the first cart stops.
whyNot.2: Uses the momentum value (6.0) as a speed.
whyNot.3: If both carts were still, momentum would have vanished, which cannot happen.

reteach.title: The egg toss
reteach.question: In an egg toss, why do the winners let their hands swing back as they catch?

blocks.h: Same egg, same momentum, more time
blocks.body: A flying egg has a fixed momentum, and every catch must remove all of it: the impulse is the same however you catch. A stiff catch removes it in a split second, which takes a big force, and the shell cracks. Swinging the hands back spreads the same impulse over a longer time, so the force on the shell is small. Air bags and crash mats use exactly this trick.

blocks.text: Soft catches do not make the momentum change smaller. They spread the same change over more time.

explain.body: Mass and speed both count. A slow heavy object can have more momentum than a fast light one.

test.q: Which of these has the most momentum?
test.why: p = mv: walker 60 × 1.5 = 90 kg·m/s; dog 40; ball 4.5; parked car 0.

whyNot.0: A fast ball has little mass: 0.15 × 30 = 4.5 kg·m/s.
whyNot.3: An object at rest has zero momentum, however massive.

explain.body: F = Δp ÷ t. Divide the change in momentum by the time to get the average force.

test.q: A 0.20 kg ball's momentum changes by 4.0 kg·m/s during a 0.050 s kick. What average force acts on it?

whyNot.1: Divides Δp by the mass (4.0 ÷ 0.20) instead of the time.

explain.body: Total momentum before = total after. When objects stick, divide the total momentum by the combined mass.

test.q: A 2.0 kg cart moving at 6.0 m/s hits a 1.0 kg cart at rest, and they stick together. What is their speed afterward?
test.why: Total p = 2.0 × 6.0 = 12 kg·m/s. Joined mass = 3.0 kg, so v = 12 ÷ 3.0 = 4.0 m/s.

whyNot.0: The added mass must slow the pair down.
whyNot.1: Gives the momentum value (12) as a speed.
whyNot.2: Averages the speeds (6.0 and 0) instead of conserving momentum.

explain.body: Momentum is always conserved in a collision. Kinetic energy is conserved only if the collision is elastic; sticking together loses the most.

test.q: Which collision loses the greatest share of its kinetic energy?
options: One where the objects stick together
One where the objects bounce apart elastically
One between two ideal billiard balls
test.why: A perfectly inelastic collision, in which the objects stick together, loses the most kinetic energy.

whyNot.1: Gas-molecule collisions are treated as elastic: no kinetic energy lost.
whyNot.3: Ideal billiard-ball collisions are treated as elastic.
